narrative.h2: Visualizers are abstract video with one job: listen back

sections.heading: What a visualizer is
sections.body: Music visualizer is the format where the visual is audio-reactive abstract motion with no narrative, character, or place - pure response to frequency and amplitude. The lineage runs from Oskar Fischinger's 1930s abstract films through the 1990s Winamp era through today's Spotify Canvas loops and YouTube release-day visualizers. The job is to give listeners something to look at that breathes with the song, often as a holding pattern on a YouTube upload or as Spotify's looping vertical art.

sections.heading: When to use it
sections.body: Visualizers are the right format for instrumental and electronic releases, lo-fi hip-hop streams, Spotify Canvas (8-second vertical loops on every track), YouTube static-image-killer release-day uploads, and anything where shipping fast matters more than narrative. The aesthetic lineage runs from Oskar Fischinger through 1990s Winamp to today's Canvas. The toolchain canon: Andrew Kramer's Video Copilot, Trapcode Particular by Peder Norrby, Robert Hodgin's Trail generative art, Beeple's Cinema 4D dailies. Acts that built brands on visualizer aesthetic: Lorn, Bonobo, Tycho's ISO50 design work, the Lofi Girl / ChilledCow YouTube ecosystem animated by Juan Pablo Machado. Anyone shipping monthly singles needs a visualizer pipeline.

sections.heading: Tunee prompting tip
sections.body: Tell Tunee the format explicitly: 'looping 8-second Spotify Canvas, 9:16 vertical, seamless loop'. Specify the reactive element: 'particle density responds to low-end, color shifts on high-end transients'. Pick one motion primitive - fluid, particle, geometry, or oscilloscope - not all four. Add 'subtle motion, holds for repeat viewing' for Canvas; 'big build matching arrangement' for full-length YouTube. Tunee renders 16:9 and 9:16 from one generation, so you get YouTube and Canvas in one pass.
